newsitem.title: USA: Hedge fund Thai victory may be pyrrhic--US experts.
newsitem.headline: Hedge fund Thai victory may be pyrrhic--US experts.

text.p: Did the hedge funds score another high profile victory in the attack on the Thai baht?
U.S. analysts said that scorecard still has to be tallied.
"The hedge funds may have won the war but lost the battle," said Feroz Talyarkhan, a managing director at Bear, Stearns and Co Inc.

After months of a standoff with currency speculators, the Bank of Thailand on Wednesday abandoned the regime of setting the baht rate in reference to a basket of major currencies and effectively devalued the baht by some 15 percent.
The devaluation would allow many speculators to recoup some of the heavy losses they suffered since Thailand imposed exchange controls on May 15, Talyarkhan said.
But even as the baht is reset daily in a "managed float" set by market rates, the offshore and onshore markets remain segregated.
The speculators who sold the baht short in the offshore forward market have yet to close out their positions, said Jeremy Frand, currency analyst at BancBoston Securities.
"Who could they sell their positions to?" he asked.

U.S. analysts noted that most of the speculative skirmishes were fought in the forward market, where funds under the control of George Soros were said to have $4 billion in forward contracts. The bulk of the speculative positions will mature in mid-July and mid-August, they noted.
The funds could hold their positions to maturity or to leverage those positions to bet on other markets, said a portfolio manager, who declined to be named.
In either case the gains and losses were not readily apparent, he said.
The putative victory in the attack on the baht has emboldened speculators to aim at their next targets in the Philippines and Malaysia, but U.S. analysts expected the rippling effect to be limited.

The domino effect of the 1994 peso crisis that hit emerging markets from Latin America to Asia to Russia were unlikely to be repeated because of ample global liquidity at present, said BancBoston's Frand.
"Investors everywhere are hunting for yields," he said.
Joyce Chang, emering markets debt strategist at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, agreed with the assessment. "The contagion won't be significant," she said.
The speculative attack on the Philippines, in fact, opened a good buying opportunity for yield pick-up, as the Philippines could manage the spillover comfortably, she said.
Geoffrey Dennis, emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel, said the difference between the peso and the baht goes beyond global liquidity.
The peso's devaluation was perceived as the beginning of a crisis for Mexico, while the baht's float was viewed as "the final piece of bad news for Thailand," he said.

Propsects of falling interest rates are good for the beleaguered Thai economy, which has already helped restore investors' confidence. And, as a result, the stock market jumped by almost 8.0 percent, Dennis said.
Talyarkhan at Bear, Stearns was less sanguine about the Thai market, predicting a "big shakeout in the economy."

While the devaluation could enhance competitiveness of export-oriented companies, the companies that borrowed heavily in the international markets in the expansionary years now would come under even harder times, he said.
